Stage 1 · Warm-up

Good news, bad news

Six messages. Some are easy to place.

Somebody sends you this message. Is it good news, bad news, or does it depend?

There is no marked answer here. Choose what you really think.

1“I’ve got a new job in another country.”
2“Your flight has been cancelled.”
3“My sister has had twins!”
4“I’ve decided to leave the group.”
5“I’ve failed my driving test again.”
6“Guess what — I’m moving in next door!”
Compare
  • Work in pairs. Find the one message you placed differently. Say why.
  • Which of the six would you answer first? Which one is hardest to answer?
Compare
  • Compare with your teacher. Find one message you placed differently and say why.
Write it down

Choose the message you marked “it depends”. Write one sentence explaining what it depends on.

Now speak — ask and answer these questions with a partner.
Answer these two out loud before you go on.

1  What was the last good news somebody told you?

2  Are you quick or slow at sharing your own news?

Then tell the class the one most surprising thing about your partner.

Stage 3 · Grammar

just, already, yet

Same tense as the last lesson. Three small words, three different jobs and two different positions.

Read these four lines from the messages in stage 5.
  • I’ve just passed my driving test.
  • I’ve already called her.
  • Have you told your mum yet?
  • We haven’t found anything yet.
Where does yet go, and what kind of sentence is it in?
One tense, three words
WordMeaningPositionExample
justa moment agoafter have / hasShe has just arrived.
alreadysooner than expectedafter have / hasI have already seen it.
yet — questionasking if it has happenedat the endHave you eaten yet?
yet — negativenot so far, but expectedat the endHe hasn’t called yet.
Positive + yetNot possible. I have finished yet is wrong — use already.
Present Perfect recycledThe tense itself is Lesson 17: have / has + past participle, no finished time expression.
The rules that matter
  • just and already sit between have and the participle. yet sits at the end of the sentence.
  • yet only works in questions and negatives. In a positive sentence use already.
  • already in a question shows surprise: Have you finished already? means “that was fast”.
  • Do not put a finished time with these words. I’ve just arrived yesterday is wrong — yesterday forces the Past Simple.
Listen. The same three words, said twice. Which one sounds genuinely excited?

In English the feeling is in the voice, not in the words. A flat “That’s fantastic” sounds like the opposite.

Full grammar reference — Present Perfect with just, already and yet

Form

justI’ve just passed my test. (a moment ago)
alreadyShe’s already called her mother. (sooner than expected)
yet — questionHave you told her yet?
yet — negativeThey haven’t given us an answer yet.
Positionjust and already go between have and the participle; yet goes at the end.

When and why we use it

  • Just means the action finished a very short time ago.
  • Already says it happened earlier than the listener expected. It is used in positive sentences.
  • Yet says the action is expected but has not happened. It is used in questions and negatives, at the end of the sentence.
  • All three connect a past action to the present moment, which is why they take the Present Perfect.

Signal words

just · already · yet · still (not) · so far

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I have already not eaten. → I haven’t eaten yet.Yet for negatives.
  • Have you finished already? → Have you finished yet?A neutral question takes yet.
  • I have yet finished. → I have already finished.Yet never sits in that position.
  • She has just call me. → She has just called me.The participle after has.

Don’t confuse it with

Have you finished yet? is a normal question. Have you finished already? shows surprise that it was so quick.

Stage 6 · Now you

Your news, and their answer

Write it first, then say it.

1 · Write your own exchange. Use the model’s shape: news → reaction → question with yet → answer with already or just.

Two exchanges: one with good news, one with bad news. About 40–60 words each.

Phrase bank

Guess what! · Have you heard…? · I’ve just… · I’ve already… · Have you … yet? · We haven’t … yet · Congratulations! · That’s fantastic! · Oh no! · What a shame! · Never mind.

Your teacher will read it after the speaking task, not now.

Keep this and read your two exchanges back out loud.

2 · Check your own writing.
1Did you put just and already after have / has?
2Is yet at the end, and only in a question or a negative?
3Did you avoid finished time words like yesterday with the Present Perfect?
3 · Work in pairs. Take a card and give the news. Your partner reacts and asks a question with yet. Then swap cards.
Card A

Good news. You have just been offered a job in another city. You have already told your family. You have not signed anything yet.

Card B

Bad news. Your laptop has just stopped working the night before a deadline. You have already tried everything. You have not called the shop yet.

Do not read the card out. Give the news in one sentence and let your partner ask.

4 · Swap roles and give the second card’s news. This time react with your voice, not only your words.
3 · Take a card and give the news to your teacher. Your teacher reacts and asks a question with yet. Then take the second card.

Stage 7 · Wrap

You can now…

Click each line you are sure about.

  • say something happened a moment ago — I’ve just…
  • say it happened sooner than expected — I’ve already…
  • ask and say “not so far” — Have you … yet? / I haven’t … yet

  • react to both — Congratulations! That’s fantastic! Oh no! What a shame!
